title: Venus and Adonis
author: William Shakespeare
setting: A wood and meadow at the edge of a hunt, over one day, a night and the next morning
lengthNote: 1,194 lines in 199 six-line stanzas rhyming ababcc
openingLine: Even as the sun with purple-colour’d face
summary: Venus, goddess of love, falls for the young hunter Adonis as he sets out for the chase. She pulls him from his horse, holds him down, kisses him and argues with him: the god of war once begged for her love, beauty should be used before it fades, and he has a duty to father a child. Adonis blushes, sulks and refuses. His horse breaks free to chase a mare, stranding him with her, and by nightfall she has won one kiss and learned that he means to hunt the boar in the morning. He rejects her love as lust and leaves. At dawn she finds him killed by the boar. His blood becomes a purple and white flower, and Venus prophesies that love will always be joined with sorrow before she flies away to Paphos.
referenceStyle: line numbers, counting the poem's 1,194 lines

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of the Complete Works of William Shakespeare (eBook 100)
sourceText.note: Every quotation here is taken word for word from this text. Line numbers count the poem's 1,194 lines, as the text itself does beside every fourth line. It opens with Shakespeare's Latin motto from Ovid's Amores and his dedication to the Earl of Southampton.

atAGlance.label: Published
atAGlance.note: Shakespeare's first printed work, which the dedication calls the first heir of my invention.

atAGlance.label: Form
atAGlance.note: Six lines each, rhyming ababcc; the form is often called the Venus and Adonis stanza.

atAGlance.label: Source
atAGlance.note: Book 10. In Ovid, Adonis returns Venus's love; Shakespeare makes him refuse it.

atAGlance.label: Readers
atAGlance.note: Reprinted more often than any other work of Shakespeare's in his lifetime.

structure.label: Lines 1-258
structure.title: The first wooing
structure.summary: In the early morning Adonis sets out to hunt, and Venus, sick with desire, pulls him from his horse, ties the horse to a branch and pushes him to the ground. She kisses him, argues with him and weeps. She tells him the god of war was once her captive, offers her body as a park for him to graze in, warns him that beauty which is not used will rot, and tells him he has a duty to breed. He blushes, frowns and says little, complains that the sun is burning his face, and as soon as she loosens her hold he makes for his horse.

scenes.title: The hunter and the goddess
scenes.summary: Adonis loves hunting and laughs at love; Venus comes at him like a bold suitor.

scenes.title: Pulled from the saddle
scenes.summary: She tethers his horse, pushes him down and kisses him like a hungry eagle.

scenes.title: Mars
scenes.summary: The god of war was her captive once, led in a chain of roses.

scenes.title: The duty to breed
scenes.summary: Torches are made to light, and beauty is made to be passed on.

scenes.title: The park
scenes.summary: She offers herself as a park and him as her deer.

structure.label: Lines 259-324
structure.title: The horse and the jennet
structure.summary: A breeding mare comes out of a copse. Adonis's horse breaks his rein and his girths and goes after her, and the narrator describes him point by point, as a painter would. The mare plays cold and kicks at him, then grows kinder, and the two gallop off into the wood together, leaving Adonis on foot.

scenes.title: The stallion
scenes.summary: The horse breaks free for the mare, and the narrator paints him feature by feature.

scenes.title: Into the wood
scenes.summary: The mare is cold, then kind, and the two run off together.

structure.label: Lines 325-588
structure.title: The second wooing
structure.summary: Adonis sits down in a temper, and Venus tries again. She kneels, takes his hand, and at last he speaks, telling her to let him go. She holds up the runaway horse as an example of natural desire; he answers that a colt broken too young never grows strong. When he frowns she falls as if dead, and he slaps her cheeks, chafes her lips and kisses her to bring her round. Night comes. He agrees to a goodnight kiss, she pulls him down and kisses him until he is exhausted, and when she asks to meet tomorrow he tells her he is going to hunt the boar.

scenes.title: The hand
scenes.summary: Venus kneels, takes his hand, and Adonis finally speaks.

scenes.title: The faint
scenes.summary: She falls as if dead, and he revives her with a kiss.

scenes.title: Goodnight
scenes.summary: A parting kiss, a struggle, and the news of tomorrow's hunt.

structure.label: Lines 589-816
structure.title: The boar
structure.summary: At the word boar Venus turns pale and pulls him down on top of her. She describes the boar's tusks and bristles, imagines Adonis dead beneath it, and begs him to hunt the hare instead, telling the story of poor Wat doubling back to escape the hounds. Then she returns to her argument that beauty must breed. Adonis answers that what she calls love is lust, which has taken love's name, and he runs off home through the dark.

scenes.title: The boar described
scenes.summary: Venus's fear, the tusks, jealousy the informer, and a vision of Adonis dead.

scenes.title: Poor Wat
scenes.summary: The hunted hare, doubling back to escape the hounds.

scenes.title: Love and lust
scenes.summary: Adonis answers at length and runs home in the dark.

structure.label: Lines 817-1026
structure.title: Night and the hunt
structure.summary: Venus spends the night alone lamenting, answered only by echoes. At dawn she hears the hounds at bay and knows they have found a dangerous quarry. She sees the boar with its mouth red, finds wounded hounds, and curses Death. A distant huntsman's call gives her hope, and she takes back everything she said about Death and blames the boar instead.

scenes.title: Night
scenes.summary: Echoes all night, and the lark at dawn.

scenes.title: The hounds at bay
scenes.summary: The boar's red mouth, the wounded hounds, and Venus's curse on Death.

scenes.title: Hope
scenes.summary: She takes back the curse, flatters Death, and blames the boar.

structure.label: Lines 1027-1194
structure.title: Death and the flower
structure.summary: Running towards a horn, she finds Adonis gored in the flank by the boar. She laments over him, imagines that the boar meant only to kiss him, and prophesies that love will from now on be attended by sorrow. His body melts away, and a purple flower chequered with white springs from his blood. Venus picks it, says she will keep it in her breast, and flies to Paphos in her chariot drawn by doves.

scenes.title: The wound
scenes.summary: She finds him gored and imagines the boar meant to kiss him.

scenes.title: The prophecy
scenes.summary: Sorrow on love hereafter shall attend.

scenes.title: The flower
scenes.summary: A purple flower from his blood, and Venus's flight to Paphos.

characters.name: Venus
characters.summary: The goddess of love, who cannot make one boy love her. She pulls Adonis from his horse, holds him down, kisses him, and argues with every means she has: flattery, tears, a faint, the example of Mars, and the claim that beauty must breed. When he is killed she grieves, prophesies that love will always be joined with sorrow, and takes the flower that grows from his blood.
characters.clue: She once led the god of war prisoner in a chain of red roses, and cannot persuade one boy to kiss her.

characters.name: Adonis
characters.summary: A beautiful young man who loves hunting and laughs at love. He blushes, frowns and says little, and when he does speak he argues that he is too young and that what Venus calls love is lust. He goes to hunt the boar against her warning and is killed by it, and his blood becomes a purple and white flower.
characters.clue: He says he knows not love, unless it is a boar, and then he chases it.

characters.name: The narrator
characters.summary: The voice that tells the story, with relish and some irony. The narrator pities and teases Venus, draws long similes from hunting and country life, and describes Adonis's horse as a painter would.
characters.clue: Calls the goddess poor queen of love, and compares her kisses to a starving eagle tearing at its prey.

characters.name: The stallion
characters.summary: Tied to a branch while Venus woos his master, he breaks his rein at the sight of a breeding mare, chases her and runs off with her into the wood. He does everything Adonis will not, and Venus holds him up as an example.
characters.clue: He crushes the iron bit between his teeth and leaves his master on foot.

relationships.label: does what his master will not

characters.name: The jennet
characters.summary: She comes out of a copse and attracts Adonis's horse. At first she puts on a show of coldness and kicks at him, then grows kinder and runs off into the wood with him.
characters.clue: She kicks at a suitor's embraces, then grows kinder and runs off with him into the wood.

characters.name: The boar
characters.summary: Venus describes him before he appears: a battle of bristles on his back, tusks that are never sheathed, eyes like glow-worms, and a snout that digs graves. At dawn his mouth is red with blood, and he has gored Adonis in the groin. Venus imagines that he only meant to kiss him.
characters.clue: His snout digs sepulchres wherever he goes, and at dawn his mouth is painted red.

characters.name: Wat
characters.summary: The hare Venus describes when she begs Adonis to hunt something harmless. Chased by hounds, he doubles back and runs among sheep, rabbits and deer to hide his scent, and stops on a hill to listen like a sick man hearing the passing bell.
characters.clue: A hunted creature who hides among sheep and deer to confuse the hounds, then stands on a hill to listen.

characters.name: Death
characters.summary: Finding the hounds wounded, Venus turns on Death as a grim-grinning ghost that has killed Adonis by mistake, aiming at old age and hitting a child. When she hears a huntsman and hopes Adonis is alive, she begs Death's pardon and flatters him as king of graves.
characters.clue: Called a grim-grinning ghost and earth's worm, then flattered as king of graves.

themes.name: Desire and refusal
themes.summary: Venus's desire is enormous and inventive, and it meets a steady no. She pulls Adonis from his horse, holds him down and kisses him while he tries to leave, and the poem never lets us forget his refusal, however comic her persistence becomes.
themes.development: Only the horses show desire returned, and Venus's use of them as an argument does not persuade Adonis.

themes.name: The wooer and the wooed
themes.summary: The poem reverses the usual roles of love poetry. A mature goddess woos a young man with the arguments men used on women, and he blushes, sulks and pleads to be let go, as the lady of a sonnet might.
themes.development: The reversal supplies much of the comedy, and it also lets readers see familiar methods of courtship from the other side.

themes.name: Love against lust
themes.summary: Venus calls what she feels love, and Adonis calls it lust, which has usurped love's name. His speech on the difference, with love like sunshine after rain and lust like tempest after sun, is the poem's clearest statement of the argument.
themes.development: Venus's prophecy at the end concedes part of his case: love from now on will be jealous, deceitful and mixed with sorrow.

themes.name: Beauty, breeding and time
themes.summary: Venus argues that beauty must be used before it fades and that Adonis owes the world a child, the same case the first seventeen of Shakespeare's sonnets make to a young man. Adonis answers that he is unripe fruit.
themes.development: The boar ends the argument. The beauty Venus urged him to pass on dies with him, and she says black Chaos comes again.

themes.name: The hunter hunted
themes.summary: Adonis wants to hunt, and Venus hunts him. The poem is full of predators and prey: an eagle tearing at its catch, a bird in a net, a deer in a park, the hare Wat doubling back from the hounds, and the boar.
themes.development: The hunter ends as the quarry, gored by the boar he chose over Venus, and she imagines the tusk as a kiss.

themes.name: Grief and loss
themes.summary: The last third of the poem is grief: a night of lament answered only by echoes, a curse on Death taken back as soon as hope returns, and the discovery of the body. Her feelings swing so violently that the narrator calls love ridiculous in its despair and hope.
themes.development: Her grief ends in withdrawal: she keeps the flower in her breast and flies to Paphos to hide.

themes.name: Transformation
themes.summary: As in Ovid, the story ends in a metamorphosis. Adonis's body melts away and a purple and white flower springs from his blood, and Venus treats the flower as his child and keeps it in her breast.
themes.development: Shakespeare adds a second transformation, of love itself, which after Venus's prophecy will always be mixed with sorrow.

techniques.name: The six-line stanza
techniques.definition: A stanza of four alternately rhyming lines followed by a rhyming couplet (ababcc).
techniques.inThisBook: All 199 stanzas use it. The first four lines set out a picture or an argument and the couplet turns it, often with a joke, so the poem moves forward six lines at a time.

techniques.name: Extended simile
techniques.definition: A comparison worked out over several lines.
techniques.inThisBook: The narrator compares Venus to a starving eagle, Adonis to a bird in a net and a dive-dapper ducking under a wave, and Venus's eyes to a snail's horns shrinking back, often introducing the comparison with Look how.

techniques.name: The blazon
techniques.definition: A list praising a body feature by feature.
techniques.inThisBook: Venus lists her own perfections to Adonis, and the narrator lists the horse's, from round hoof to tender hide, in the same form.

techniques.name: Apostrophe
techniques.definition: Addressing someone absent or dead, or a thing or idea, as if it could hear.
techniques.inThisBook: Venus harangues Death as a grim-grinning ghost and then apologises to it. She also addresses the rising sun, and at the end the flower.

techniques.name: Personification
techniques.definition: Giving human qualities to an idea or thing.
techniques.inThisBook: Jealousy is an informer and a spy, the sun wishes he were in Adonis's place beside Venus, and the earth trips Adonis in the dark because it wants a kiss.

techniques.name: Classical allusion
techniques.definition: A reference to the myths and literature of Greece and Rome.
techniques.inThisBook: The whole poem retells Ovid, and Venus's arguments call on Mars, Narcissus and Tantalus. It ends with her flight to Paphos, her sacred city.

techniques.name: Antithesis
techniques.definition: Opposed ideas set against each other in balanced phrases.
techniques.inThisBook: The argument is built from oppositions: heat and frost, red for desire and red for shame, love and lust, sunshine and tempest.

techniques.name: Extended conceit
techniques.definition: A comparison developed at length, often between unlike things.
techniques.inThisBook: Venus maps her body as a deer park with hills, fountains and brakes, and the goodnight kiss becomes a siege in which her lips conquer and his pay ransom.

techniques.name: Animal imagery
techniques.inThisBook: Eagle, dive-dapper, bird, deer, colt, hare, snail and boar all stand in for the two lovers, and the horses act out the desire Adonis refuses.

techniques.name: Red and white
techniques.definition: Colours used as a code for feeling, especially the blush and the pallor of a face.
techniques.inThisBook: Adonis blushes red with shame and Venus with desire, she turns pale at the word boar, his wound drenches lily white in purple, and the flower that grows from his blood is purple chequered with white.

techniques.name: Prophecy
techniques.definition: A prediction spoken within the work.
techniques.inThisBook: Venus's curse at the end, stanza after stanza beginning It shall, foretells that love will always be joined with jealousy, deceit and sorrow.

techniques.name: Wordplay
techniques.inThisBook: Deer and dear, begot and get, will three times in one couplet, and king of graves turned round into grave for kings.

quotations.text: Rose-cheek’d Adonis tried him to the chase; Hunting he lov’d, but love he laugh’d to scorn;
quotations.speaker: Narrator
quotations.context: The opening stanza, as Adonis rides out in the morning.
quotations.analysis: The second line turns on itself: he loved hunting and scorned love. The whole poem follows from that reversal, since Adonis will be pursued by the love he laughs at and killed by the hunt he prefers.

quotations.text: Sick-thoughted Venus makes amain unto him, And like a bold-fac’d suitor ’gins to woo him.
quotations.speaker: Narrator
quotations.context: The couplet of the first stanza.
quotations.analysis: The first couplet makes the goddess the wooer and the boy the wooed. A bold-faced suitor was a man's part, and the two-syllable rhyme of unto him and woo him gives the poem a comic lilt from the start.

quotations.text: Ten kisses short as one, one long as twenty:
quotations.speaker: Venus
quotations.context: Promising Adonis what he will have if he dismounts.
quotations.analysis: Venus offers to make time behave for them, with ten kisses as short as one and one as long as twenty. The mirrored numbers show her gift for rhetoric, which she uses all through the poem without ever getting what she wants.

quotations.text: She red and hot as coals of glowing fire, He red for shame, but frosty in desire.
quotations.speaker: Narrator
quotations.context: Venus has pulled Adonis from his horse and holds him under one arm.
quotations.analysis: Both of them are red, for opposite reasons. The couplet sets heat against frost and makes the poem's colour code plain: her red is desire, his is shame.

quotations.text: Backward she push’d him, as she would be thrust, And govern’d him in strength, though not in lust.
quotations.speaker: Narrator
quotations.context: Venus has tied up the horse and turns to the rider.
quotations.analysis: The narrator's joke is that Venus puts him in the position she wishes he would put her in. She can overpower him but cannot make him want her, and the second line separates strength from desire in exactly those terms.

quotations.text: Even as an empty eagle, sharp by fast, Tires with her beak on feathers, flesh and bone,
quotations.speaker: Narrator
quotations.context: Describing how Venus kisses Adonis as he lies on the ground.
quotations.analysis: Tires means tears at, as a hawk tears its prey. In the simile the goddess of love becomes a starving predator and Adonis the carcass, and from here on the hunting images put him again and again in the place of the hunted.

quotations.text: Look how a bird lies tangled in a net, So fasten’d in her arms Adonis lies;
quotations.speaker: Narrator
quotations.context: Adonis lies trapped in Venus's embrace.
quotations.analysis: Look how is a formula the narrator returns to whenever a comparison is coming. Here the hunter is caught like a bird in a fowler's net, one more reversal of who hunts whom.

quotations.text: Leading him prisoner in a red rose chain:
quotations.speaker: Venus
quotations.context: Telling Adonis that Mars, the god of war, was once her captive.
quotations.analysis: The chain of red roses gives love the trappings of military conquest. Venus means the boast to shame Adonis into yielding, and it shows how unused she is to being refused.

quotations.text: Love is a spirit all compact of fire, Not gross to sink, but light, and will aspire.
quotations.speaker: Venus
quotations.context: Arguing that her love is no burden to him.
quotations.analysis: Venus describes love as the lightest of the elements, rising like flame. The poem's picture of her, sweating, heavy with desire and holding a boy down, makes the claim hard to accept, and in the next stanza she lies on a primrose bank to prove it.

quotations.text: Narcissus so himself himself forsook, And died to kiss his shadow in the brook.
quotations.speaker: Venus
quotations.context: Accusing Adonis of loving only himself.
quotations.analysis: Venus cites the youth in Ovid who fell in love with his own reflection and died of it. The doubled himself himself makes the grammar fold in on itself, as Narcissus did.

quotations.text: Seeds spring from seeds, and beauty breedeth beauty; Thou wast begot; to get it is thy duty.
quotations.speaker: Venus
quotations.context: The end of her argument that beauty must be used.
quotations.analysis: Here Venus makes the case Shakespeare's first seventeen sonnets make to a young man: beauty must be passed on to a child or it is wasted. With the pun on begot and get, being born is a debt.

quotations.text: I’ll be a park, and thou shalt be my deer;
quotations.speaker: Venus
quotations.context: She has locked her arms around him like a fence.
quotations.analysis: A park was an enclosed hunting ground. Venus maps her body as a landscape of hills, fountains and brakes for him to graze in, and the pun on deer and dear keeps the hunt and the courtship in the same line.

quotations.text: Round-hoof’d, short-jointed, fetlocks shag and long, Broad breast, full eye, small head, and nostril wide,
quotations.speaker: Narrator
quotations.context: Describing Adonis's horse as it courts the mare.
quotations.analysis: The horse gets the feature-by-feature praise a sonnet gives a mistress. It also reads like a horse-dealer's checklist, and the stanza ends by noting that he lacks only a proud rider on his back.

quotations.text: The sea hath bounds, but deep desire hath none;
quotations.speaker: Venus
quotations.context: Using the runaway horse to excuse desire.
quotations.analysis: Venus treats the horse as proof that desire cannot be held back. The line works as a maxim, and it also admits the problem: her desire has no limit, and Adonis's refusal is not allowed to be one.

quotations.text: The colt that’s back’d and burden’d being young, Loseth his pride, and never waxeth strong.
quotations.speaker: Adonis
quotations.context: Answering her example of the horse.
quotations.analysis: Adonis answers the horse with a horse of his own. He argues that he is too young, like a colt broken to the saddle too early, and turns Venus's example of animal nature against her.

quotations.text: He kisses her; and she, by her good will, Will never rise, so he will kiss her still.
quotations.speaker: Narrator
quotations.context: Venus has fallen as if dead, and Adonis tries to revive her.
quotations.analysis: The couplet's joke is that the cure works too well: she would stay down for ever to keep him kissing, and will turns up three times in two lines.

quotations.text: The mellow plum doth fall, the green sticks fast, Or being early pluck’d, is sour to taste.
quotations.speaker: Adonis
quotations.context: Asking her to measure his strangeness by his unripe years.
quotations.analysis: Adonis's second answer is again about age: he is unripe fruit, and fruit picked green is sour. He speaks more briefly than Venus, and more sharply.

quotations.text: Her lips are conquerors, his lips obey, Paying what ransom the insulter willeth;
quotations.speaker: Narrator
quotations.context: The goodnight kiss Adonis has agreed to.
quotations.analysis: The kiss becomes a military occupation, with Venus as the conqueror and Adonis paying ransom. An insulter was one who triumphs over a beaten enemy.

quotations.text: She’s love, she loves, and yet she is not lov’d.
quotations.speaker: Narrator
quotations.context: After Adonis has told her he will hunt the boar.
quotations.analysis: The line uses love three ways: her name, her action and what she cannot get. It sums up both the comedy and the pathos of the poem, in which the goddess of love is the one figure who is not loved.

quotations.text: This sour informer, this bate-breeding spy, This canker that eats up love’s tender spring,
quotations.speaker: Venus
quotations.context: Explaining why the mention of the boar frightened her.
quotations.analysis: Venus personifies jealousy as an informer, a troublemaking spy and a canker worm. The string of names looks forward to her prophecy at the end, where love is to be waited on with jealousy.

quotations.text: By this, poor Wat, far off upon a hill, Stands on his hinder legs with list’ning ear,
quotations.speaker: Venus
quotations.context: Describing a hare hunt, which she urges on Adonis as safer than the boar.
quotations.analysis: Wat was a country name for the hare. Venus means the story as a lesson in safe hunting, but she tells it from the hare’s side, and the frightened, listening animal is how Adonis will end: hunted, not hunting.

quotations.text: Love comforteth like sunshine after rain, But lust’s effect is tempest after sun;
quotations.speaker: Adonis
quotations.context: In his longest speech, answering her argument.
quotations.analysis: Adonis sets love against lust line by line, and in this stanza the balance is exact. His charge is that Venus calls lust by love's name, and it gives the poem its central argument.

quotations.text: Look how a bright star shooteth from the sky, So glides he in the night from Venus’ eye.
quotations.speaker: Narrator
quotations.context: Adonis breaks away and runs home in the dark.
quotations.analysis: Coleridge quoted this couplet in Biographia Literaria as an example of an image shaped by feeling. The boy is seen as Venus sees him, a bright thing disappearing into the dark.

quotations.text: They bid thee crop a weed, thou pluck’st a flower.
quotations.speaker: Venus
quotations.context: Cursing Death, whom she believes has killed Adonis.
quotations.analysis: Venus accuses Death of picking the wrong plant. The line anticipates the ending, where Adonis really does become a flower and Venus plucks it.

quotations.text: She clepes him king of graves, and grave for kings, Imperious supreme of all mortal things.
quotations.speaker: Narrator
quotations.context: Hoping Adonis is alive after all, Venus flatters the Death she has just cursed.
quotations.analysis: Clepes means calls. The reversed phrase king of graves, and grave for kings shows how quickly Venus's rhetoric can change direction when her hopes do.

quotations.text: For he being dead, with him is beauty slain, And beauty dead, black Chaos comes again.
quotations.speaker: Venus
quotations.context: Telling herself Adonis cannot be dead.
quotations.analysis: Venus imagines the world falling back into the disorder that came before creation if he dies. Othello uses the same words of his love for Desdemona: when I love thee not, Chaos is come again.

quotations.text: So at his bloody view her eyes are fled Into the deep dark cabins of her head.
quotations.speaker: Narrator
quotations.context: Venus has just seen the boar's conquest.
quotations.analysis: The stanza before compares her eyes to a snail's tender horns, which shrink back into the shell when touched. The couplet completes the comparison, and the small, exact image slows the poem at the moment of discovery, before the grief breaks out.

quotations.text: Had I been tooth’d like him, I must confess, With kissing him I should have kill’d him first;
quotations.speaker: Venus
quotations.context: She has imagined that the boar was trying to kiss Adonis when it gored him.
quotations.analysis: Now she puts herself in the boar's place, and the poem's two kinds of pursuit, the goddess's and the beast's, meet in one confession.

quotations.text: Since thou art dead, lo here I prophesy, Sorrow on love hereafter shall attend:
quotations.speaker: Venus
quotations.context: Over the body of Adonis.
quotations.analysis: Venus’s private loss becomes a law for everyone. The prophecy that follows lists the ways love will go wrong, and explains, in the manner of Ovid, why love has been painful ever since.

quotations.text: It shall be fickle, false and full of fraud,
quotations.speaker: Venus
quotations.context: The second stanza of the prophecy.
quotations.analysis: Each stanza of the prophecy begins It shall, and the alliteration of fickle, false and full of fraud gives the curse the sound of a spell. The list that follows sets every good of love against its opposite.

quotations.text: And in his blood that on the ground lay spill’d, A purple flower sprung up, chequer’d with white,
quotations.speaker: Narrator
quotations.context: Adonis's body has melted from Venus's sight.
quotations.analysis: His red and white, the blush and pallor the poem has dwelt on since its first stanzas, become the colours of a flower. In Ovid, Venus sprinkles nectar on the blood to raise the flower; here it springs up by itself.

quotations.text: There shall not be one minute in an hour Wherein I will not kiss my sweet love’s flower.
quotations.speaker: Venus
quotations.context: Placing the flower in her breast.
quotations.analysis: Venus at last has something of Adonis that cannot refuse her. The promise to kiss the flower every minute is tender, and it is also a final echo of the kisses he tried to escape.

quotations.text: Holding their course to Paphos, where their queen Means to immure herself and not be seen.
quotations.speaker: Narrator
quotations.context: The last lines of the poem.
quotations.analysis: Paphos in Cyprus was Venus's sacred city. The poem that began with her bursting in on a hunt ends with her shutting herself away, and its last word is seen.

timeline.label: Golding's Ovid
timeline.detail: Arthur Golding's English translation of the Metamorphoses, which Shakespeare knew alongside the Latin.

timeline.label: Lodge's Scillaes Metamorphosis
timeline.detail: An Ovidian love poem in the same six-line stanza, usually counted the first of the fashion for such poems.

timeline.label: The theatres close
timeline.detail: Plague shut London's playhouses for most of 1592 to 1594, the years in which Shakespeare wrote both his narrative poems.

timeline.label: First printed
timeline.detail: Entered for publication on 18 April and printed by Richard Field, a printer from Stratford, with a dedication to the Earl of Southampton.

timeline.label: The Rape of Lucrece
timeline.detail: Shakespeare's second narrative poem, commonly taken as the graver labour promised in the first dedication, also printed by Field and dedicated to Southampton.

timeline.label: Meres's praise
timeline.detail: Francis Meres wrote that the soul of Ovid lived in mellifluous and honey-tongued Shakespeare, witness his Venus and Adonis and his Lucrece.

timeline.label: Under the pillow
timeline.detail: In The Return from Parnassus, a Cambridge student play of about 1600, a foolish gallant says he will keep Venus and Adonis under his pillow.

timeline.label: Coleridge's Biographia Literaria
timeline.detail: Coleridge used the poem to describe the signs of poetic genius in the young Shakespeare.

places.name: Paphos
places.note: Venus's sacred city in Cyprus, where she flies at the end.

places.name: London
places.note: Printed by Richard Field and sold in St Paul's Churchyard, the centre of the book trade.

places.name: Stratford-upon-Avon
places.note: Home town of both Shakespeare and his printer, Richard Field.

criticalViews.summary: Many readers take the poem as a witty, erotic entertainment in the fashion of the 1590s, written to please a young aristocratic patron and a public that bought it in edition after edition.
criticalViews.counter: The ending is not comic. Adonis dies, and with Venus’s prophecy the poem becomes an account of why love hurts.

criticalViews.summary: Recent criticism stresses that Venus physically restrains Adonis and overrides his refusals, and reads the gender reversal as a way of making coercion visible.
criticalViews.counter: Others argue that the comedy depends on Venus's helplessness: the goddess of love cannot get what she wants, and the joke is on her.

criticalViews.summary: Venus's case that beauty must reproduce links the poem to the procreation sonnets, and some critics read it as a serious argument about nature and time.
criticalViews.counter: Adonis's reply, that her love is lust and he is too young, has the last word in the debate, and the boar puts an end to the question.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare present Venus?
plan: Begin with the reversal in the first stanza, where the goddess is a bold-faced suitor.
Analyse her arguments: Mars, the park, the duty to breed.
Look at how the narrator describes her, in images of predators and as poor queen of love.
Examine her grief, from the curse on Death to the discovery of the body.
Conclude on the prophecy and whether the poem sympathises with her.

essayQuestions.question: How does the poem use animals?
plan: Start with the similes of the first wooing: eagle, bird in a net, dive-dapper.
Analyse the stallion and the jennet as an example Venus uses and Adonis rejects.
Consider Wat the hare and what Venus's story reveals.
Examine the boar and Venus's claim that it meant to kiss Adonis.
Conclude on what the animals say about human desire.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare set love against lust?
plan: Begin with Venus's claim that love is a spirit all compact of fire.
Consider how the narrator describes Venus's desire in the goodnight kiss.
Examine the prophecy of what love will be from now on.
Conclude on whether the poem sides with either speaker.

discussionQuestions: Is Venus comic, pitiable or threatening?
Why does Adonis say so little?
Why does Shakespeare spend sixty-six lines on a horse?
Does the gender reversal make the poem more troubling or less?
Is Venus's prophecy fair to love?
Why does the poem end with Venus hiding herself away?

related.why: Shakespeare's other narrative poem, dedicated to the same patron a year later.
The first seventeen sonnets make Venus's argument that beauty must breed.
Another Ovidian story in which a woman chases a man who does not want her.
The two narrative poems together in one volume.
